analysis.one_liner: Requires colleges to disclose how they pick recommended student lenders and bans lender gifts and payments to aid offices.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees in 2007 and never reached a House vote before that Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required colleges that recommend student loan lenders to publish a written selection policy and recommend at least three independent lenders. It would have forced colleges to tell students they may use any lender, how much federal aid is available, and what attendance costs, and to adopt codes of conduct barring employees from taking gifts, fees, or stock deals from loan companies. It would also have banned colleges from taking lender payments for preferred-lender status or lender-staffed aid offices, and required private loan companies to warn borrowers that federal student loans often have better terms before the borrower signs.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and parents borrowing for college. They would learn that they cannot be forced to use a college's recommended lenders, see a plain-language comparison of federal versus private loan terms before signing anything, and know the maximum federal grants and loans available. The ban on lender gifts and payments would cut the financial ties that can steer students toward costlier loans.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students and parents borrowing for college

how_it_helps.text: Colleges could not recommend lenders without a written, publicly disclosed selection policy and a minimum of three unaffiliated lenders, reducing steering toward a favored company.

Colleges would have to tell students they may use any eligible lender, that the school must process that lender's paperwork, and disclose the maximum federal grant and loan aid and the full cost of attendance.

College employees, trustees, and directors would be barred from accepting gifts, consulting fees, or stock-purchase opportunities from lenders or guaranty agencies, and colleges could not accept lender payments in exchange for recommended-lender status or lender help staffing aid offices and call centers.

Private loan companies would have to tell borrowers, before they sign, that they may qualify for federal aid and that federal student loans often carry lower rates and fees, with a signed acknowledgment that the borrower read the notice.

analysis.who_pays: Student loan companies lose paid placements on college recommended-lender lists, staffing arrangements with aid offices, and some borrowers who would otherwise take a costlier private loan instead of a federal one. Colleges bear the cost of writing, publishing, and enforcing codes of conduct and the required disclosures.
analysis.who_pays_short: Student loan lenders and college aid offices

drawbacks.text: Colleges would face real administrative costs: drafting and publishing selection policies and codes of conduct, annual compliance training for aid staff, and expanded disclosures on websites and in every financial aid mailing.

The required disclosure form covers only the lenders a college recommends, so it would standardize information within the recommended list but would not itself compare that list against every lender on the market.
Banning lender-paid staffing assistance removes a source of free help that some smaller aid offices relied on, though the bill carves out training and counseling materials with lender identification.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to borrowers are concrete and the costs modest: clearer loan comparisons, a legal right to use any lender, and fewer financial ties between loan companies and the people who steer students to them. The main burden is paperwork for colleges and lost marketing perks for lenders. A reasonable objection is that disclosure rules only work if students actually read them, and the bill's strongest fix, the ban on paid lender placements, was the part most likely to draw industry resistance.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees, which passed it down to their subcommittees, and it was never brought up for a vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Howard P. "Buck" McKeon introduced the bill in the House on April 23, 2007, joined by Rep. Ric Keller of Florida, both Republicans.
The House referred it to the Education and Labor Committee and the Financial Services Committee on the day it was introduced.

On June 7, 2007, it was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, and on July 9, 2007, to the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Higher Education, Lifelong Learning, and Competitiveness.
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote was ever scheduled, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2009, with the bill still in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student loan companies and colleges came out ahead: with no law enacted, lenders kept paid preferred-lender placements, staffing arrangements with aid offices, and gift and consulting relationships with financial aid officials for the rest of the Congress, and colleges faced no federal disclosure or code-of-conduct mandate from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lenders and colleges with existing loan arrangements

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 23, 2007, sent it to its Higher Education subcommittee on July 9, 2007, and never reported the bill to the House floor.

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 23, 2007, sent it to its Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit subcommittee on June 7, 2007, and never reported the bill to the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were House Republicans, but the bill never reached a floor vote, so no record exists of how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Student loan lenders (federally guaranteed and private)
industries.note: Lenders could no longer pay for spots on college recommended-lender lists, staff aid offices and call centers, or give gifts and consulting fees to aid officials, and would have to warn private-loan borrowers that federal loans often cost less. Their advantage came from steering students, so their loss was the borrower's gain.

Schools would bear new compliance costs for written policies, codes of conduct, annual training, and expanded disclosures, and would lose lender-paid staffing help and other lender benefits some aid offices accepted. Because some of those lender payments came at the expense of students' loan choices, the industry's interest in this bill ran against borrowers.

Guaranty agencies and servicers would be covered by the gift and conflict-of-interest limits and would be consulted on the new disclosure forms, adding compliance obligations but no direct revenue loss of the kind faced by lenders paying for placements.
